title: Iran's Guards say supertanker sank after hitting mine; India reports tanker attack near Hormuz
dek: The Revolutionary Guards claimed a tanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude went down on an 'unauthorised' route. A maritime monitor said Indian shipping authorities had reported an attack on a tanker nearby, with the crew safe. Neither account has been independently confirmed.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Sunday that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil had sunk after striking a mine in the southern waters of the Gulf, near the Strait of Hormuz. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), which monitors shipping in the region, said Indian shipping authorities had reported an attack on a tanker in the Gulf just before the strait, and that the crew were accounted for and safe.

There was no independent confirmation of the sinking. UKMTO said it was not clear whether the attack reported by the Indian authorities was the same incident the IRGC described, and that the extent of damage to the vessel and any environmental impact were not yet known.

## What each side said

In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the IRGC said two tankers had hit mines while travelling on what it called an "unauthorised route" in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, and that one of them, a supertanker, had caught fire and sunk. It did not name the vessels, their owners or their flags. On Saturday, the IRGC's navy had said two tankers struck mines after switching off their tracking systems, and that two others turned back after warnings from its maritime traffic control centre, according to Iran's official news agency.

UKMTO said the tanker in the Indian report was eastbound in the Gulf, before entering the strait, when it was attacked. It advised vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity. India's shipping authorities had not published details of the vessel, its flag or its crew by early Monday.

Iran says only Iran and Oman have the right to control traffic through the strait and requires ships to use routes it authorises. The United States rejects that claim, has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and has escorted tankers through the waterway. The US military said recently that it had cleared mines from the main shipping routes, according to reports.

## Why it matters for India

About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, and a large share of India's crude and cooking gas imports come from Gulf producers whose cargoes use it. Indian seafarers make up a large part of the crews on tankers and cargo ships in the region. On 3 November an Indian national was killed when the Indian vessel MSV Al Jusufi was attacked off Limah in Oman; 13 other Indians on board were rescued, the Ministry of External Affairs said at the time.

The latest incidents follow two days in which the IRGC said it had attacked US radar installations in Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. The US military said it shot down the two drones launched on Friday, and Bahrain said its air defences intercepted the attacks on Sunday. The IRGC repeated on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz "is closed".

## What happens next

Shipping companies and insurers will be watching for confirmation of the vessel's identity from tracking data, its owners or flag state. Iran has set out seven conditions for a deal with the United States through a Qatari mediator, including lifting the naval blockade and sanctions, and is awaiting a US response, according to reports.
